title: Group Chat and Scholarship
premise: At Ashgrove Academy, Tamsin Joubert has perfected invisibility — until the school's legendary ghost, a student who died in 1974 after being silenced by the administration, begins leaving notes in impossible ink addressed to specific students by name. The notes expose buried injustices: stolen scholarships, erased students, a cover-up that made the school's founding family rich. When a note names Tamsin's late mother as one of the silenced, she joins three other 'addressed' students to uncover the truth before the school's centennial gala buries it forever. In the end, Tamsin must choose between the scholarship that guarantees her future and publishing the evidence that would burn it down — and she discovers the ghost was never supernatural at all, but a living archivist keeping a fifty-year promise.
about_author: Rosalind Winterbourne is a former debate coach who spent a decade listening to teenagers argue circles around adults who wouldn't listen back. She writes from a converted chapel in coastal Maine, where she keeps an archive of unsent letters donated by former students.

chapters.title: The Rules of Staying Small
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. We meet her winning a debate tournament while planning exactly how not to be noticed for it; at home, her father dismisses her trophy and her grief for her mother alike. Establishes her survival strategy: head down, grades up, locker shut. Emotional beat: the loneliness of being excellent on purpose.

chapters.title: Ink That Shouldn't Exist
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. A note appears inside her locked locker, addressed by name, written in ink that shifts color and won't smudge under water. It says only: 'They took your mother's name off the list.' She assumes a prank, but the handwriting unsettles her — it resembles her mother's old marginalia. Emotional beat: first crack in her armor.

chapters.title: The Legend of the Grey Girl
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She researches the school ghost: a 1974 scholarship student, Edith Marlowe, who drowned in the reservoir weeks after being expelled for 'forgery.' Official records are suspiciously thin. Her best friend Priya warns her to drop it. Emotional beat: curiosity curdling into compulsion.

chapters.title: Four Names, One Locker Row
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Tamsin discovers three others received notes: Marcus (a football star whose brother was quietly expelled), Devi (whose grandmother's name is on a stolen patent), and quiet Theo, who claims his note is blank. They form an uneasy alliance in the library basement. Emotional beat: reluctant belonging.

chapters.title: What the Yearbook Didn't Print
chapters.summary: Devi's POV. The group finds Edith's yearbook page defaced — photo cut out, achievements whited over. Devi's grandmother recognizes the name and goes silent on the phone. First hint the conspiracy reaches beyond school walls. Emotional beat: history pressing on the present.

chapters.title: Centennial Countdown
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. Headmistress Vane announces the centennial gala and a new 'Legacy Scholarship' — funded by the Ashcombe family, whose fortune built the school. Marcus realizes the scholarship he needs is the same one Edith allegedly forged documents to win. Emotional beat: hope with a hook in it.

chapters.title: The Argument at Home
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Her father finds her research and forbids it — not from indifference, but terror; he knew her mother was investigating something before she died. Their fight mirrors the debates Tamsin always wins everywhere except home. Emotional beat: love expressed as control.

chapters.title: A Second Note, A Sharper Edge
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo's blank note fills in overnight: coordinates to the reservoir boathouse. Inside, they find Edith's hidden scrapbook — clippings proving the Ashcombes stole scholarship funds and patents from students of color in the '60s and '70s. Emotional beat: awe and dread in equal measure.

chapters.title: Someone Is Watching the Watchers
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. The scrapbook vanishes from Theo's locker; Vane summons each of them individually with gentle, surgical questions about 'school spirit.' Marcus, terrified of losing his scholarship, considers trading information. Emotional beat: loyalty tested by fear.

chapters.title: The Debate Champion Loses
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin publicly challenges Vane at an assembly using flawless rhetoric — and loses, because power doesn't play fair. Humiliated, she understands the ghost's notes aren't about winning arguments but refusing to stop speaking. Emotional beat: defeat as education.

chapters.title: Her Mother's Handwriting
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Forensic comparison confirms the impossible ink matches her mother's pen — the same pen missing since the funeral. Either someone close to her family is the ghost, or her mother left something behind. Emotional beat: grief reorganized as a lead.

chapters.title: Blank Pages, Loud Boy
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo confesses why his note was blank: he's the grandson of the janitor who helped hide Edith's papers in 1974 and has known the secret his whole life, too afraid to speak. His silence becomes the group's mirror. Emotional beat: shame transformed into resolve.

chapters.title: The Archive Beneath the Chapel
chapters.summary: Devi's POV. Following her grandmother's reluctant directions, they find a sealed room beneath the old chapel containing decades of confiscated records — including a file on Tamsin's mother, opened the month she died. Emotional beat: the past is not past.

chapters.title: Vane's Version
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Vane corners Tamsin alone and tells her own story: she was once an 'addressed' student too, and chose protection over truth — and has regretted it for thirty years. She neither helps nor stops them. Emotional beat: a warning wearing a confession.

chapters.title: Marcus Breaks
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. Pressured by Vane and his family's desperation, Marcus hands over the chapel location. He immediately regrets it and warns the group, fracturing their trust. Emotional beat: betrayal and repair beginning in the same breath.

chapters.title: The Gala Trap
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The group learns the Ashcombe family will announce a donation naming the library after Edith Marlowe — laundering the lie forever. They have until the gala toast to act. Emotional beat: ticking clock.

chapters.title: Ghost, Revealed
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The 'ghost' is Ms. Okonkwo, the retired archivist, Edith's best friend, who has spent fifty years sending notes in preserved ink whenever injustice recurs — and who recruited Tamsin's mother before her death. She gives them the master ledger. Emotional beat: wonder giving way to human courage.

chapters.title: What Tamsin Decides
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Publishing means losing the Legacy Scholarship and possibly her father's job at Ashcombe. She drafts two speeches — one safe, one true — and burns neither. Emotional beat: the choice crystallizing.

chapters.title: The Toast
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. At the gala, as the Ashcombes raise their glasses, Tamsin takes the microphone meant for ceremony and reads the ledger aloud; Devi projects the archives; Theo unlocks the chapel doors; Marcus stands beside them, forfeiting his scholarship. Emotional beat: collective courage.

chapters.title: Aftermath of True Things
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Fallout: investigations launch, the Ashcombe wing is renamed, Vane resigns and leaves her own confession. Tamsin's father, shaken, finally shows her her mother's file — and apologizes for mistaking silence for safety. Emotional beat: grief met at last.

chapters.title: The Last Note
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Ms. Okonkwo passes the ink and the duty to the four of them — the archive will need keepers after her. Tamsin writes her first note and slips it into a locker belonging to a scared freshman. Emotional beat: inheritance accepted.

chapters.title: Head Up, Grades Up, Locker Open
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Months later: no scholarship, but a state debate final where she argues a case about her own school and wins — then dedicates it to Edith and her mother. She walks the halls unhidden, locker open, waiting for whoever needs a note next. Emotional beat: belonging chosen, not granted.
